showcases.name: Cobblestone → Sand Factory
showcases.blurb: A windmill-and-engine gear train drills cobblestone, mills it down through gravel into sand, and a placer sets the sand back down.
showcases.description: A complete production line. A drill chews through the cobblestone in front of it (as if fed by a cobblestone generator), and the rubble drops into a hopper and barrel. Power comes from two passive-ish sources side by side — a huge windmill and an engine, enough combined supply for the whole tower of machines — whose rotation is gathered through a clutch and a cluster of gears, then carried down vertical shafts to a pair of stacked millstones. The first millstone grinds cobblestone into gravel; the second grinds that gravel into sand. A placer at the foot of the column takes the finished sand and sets it down as a real block in the world.

showcases.name: Engine → Fan
showcases.blurb: A fuel-burning engine spins a shaft up into a fan that blows a gust of air.
showcases.description: The engine burns fuel — coal, charcoal, a lava bucket — to produce rotational power, measured in Power. That power runs up the shaft (a shaft just transmits rotation along its axis) into the fan, which turns it back into motion: a directed gust that pushes entities away from its face. The more surplus power on the network, the stronger the push.

showcases.name: Engine → Millstone
showcases.blurb: A fuel-burning engine drives a vertical shaft down into a millstone that mills items.
showcases.description: A fuelled engine sends power down a vertical shaft into a millstone. The millstone is always a Y-axis machine — it draws power from directly above or below — and grinds items fed from an adjacent container into new materials according to its recipe set while its wheel spins. Stop feeding the engine fuel and the whole column winds down.

showcases.name: Motor → Drill
showcases.blurb: A bank of five redstone motors powers a drill that bores forward through solid stone.
showcases.description: Motors are passive power sources — they spin on their own (and redstone DISABLES them, rather than enabling them) — but each one supplies just a single unit of power, and a drill demands five. So five motors sit coupled in a line, their rotation summing along the shared axle before it feeds through a clutch into the drill, which bores into whatever block sits in front of its bit, breaking it in stages. A clutch passes power straight through like a shaft, but a redstone signal disengages it — a quick way to stop the drill without unpowering the motors. Because rotation only couples along a block's spin axis, everything sits in one line.

showcases.name: Motor → Fan
showcases.blurb: A pair of redstone motors spins a shaft up into a fan that blows a gust of air — no fuel needed.
showcases.description: Passive motors spin on their own and drive a shaft up into a fan. Unlike the fuel-burning engine, motors need no upkeep — they run continuously until a redstone signal disables them. Each motor supplies one unit of power and the fan demands two, so a second motor sits coupled below the first on the same vertical axle. The fan turns that rotation into a directed gust that pushes entities away from its face.

showcases.name: Motor → Reverser → Drawbridge
showcases.blurb: A motor drives a rotator hinge through a lever-switched reverser; a pulse swings the drawbridge.
showcases.description: The rotator is a hinge: on a redstone pulse it gathers the connected planks into a moving structure and swings them as one — a drawbridge. Power reaches it from the motor behind, but passes through a reverser first: a floor lever beside the reverser is switched on, so the swing runs the reversed direction. Unlike the spinning machines, this is the mechanism system at work — real blocks are lifted into display entities, rotated, and set back down at their new orientation.

showcases.name: Motor → Ceiling Rotator
showcases.blurb: A rotator hung from the block above swings it like a hatch when pulsed — the floor door, upside down.
showcases.description: A rotator doesn't only sit on the floor: mounted against the underside of a block it hangs as a ceiling hinge, swinging the block above it (and anything glued to it) like a trapdoor. It's still a Y-axis consumer, so power arrives up the vertical axle from the motor below, while the swung block sits on the opposite (mounting) side above. A redstone pulse gives the rising edge that fires one swing.

showcases.name: Gear Corner
showcases.blurb: A motor's vertical power meshes through gears to turn a 90° corner and drive a fan sideways.
showcases.description: A shaft only carries rotation straight along its axis; gears turn the corner. Here a pair of passive motors (one power unit each — the fan demands two) spins a vertical (Y) gear, which meshes with a second gear mounted at 90° (X) beside it — a bevel pair. The horizontal gear then drives a fan on its own axis, so power that entered going up leaves going sideways.

showcases.name: Windmill → Drill
showcases.blurb: A wall-mounted huge windmill spins on the wind and bores a drill straight through solid stone.
showcases.description: Windmills are passive sources — they never need fuel or redstone, they just turn. Mounted on a wall the blades spin in a vertical plane, and (unlike a floor windmill) they deliver power horizontally along that spin axis. This one drives a shaft into a drill that bores forward through stone. Bigger banners mean a bigger windmill and far more power.

showcases.name: Motor → Press
showcases.blurb: A tower of motors drives a vertical shaft into a press whose piston bobs to squeeze a barrel's contents.
showcases.description: The press is a Y-axis machine like the millstone: it takes power from directly above and extracts juices, oils and dyes from items in the barrel it mounts on. Passive motors keep its piston bobbing without any fuel — each supplies one unit of power against the press's demand of four, so four motors stack coupled on the same vertical axle. (This demo shows the motion; a running press needs items in the barrel to actually produce anything.)

showcases.name: Water Wheel → Fan
showcases.blurb: Falling water turns a paddle wheel, which spins a shaft into a fan that blows a gust of air.
showcases.description: A water wheel is a source powered by moving water — not a still pool, but a real current pushing its paddles. A stream falls past its rim and sets it turning, and that rotation runs down a shaft into a fan. No fuel, no redstone, just flow.

showcases.name: Water Wheel & Windmill Gear Corner
showcases.blurb: A water wheel and a windmill each drive a shaft into a pair of corner-meshed gears.
showcases.description: Two passive generators meeting at a gear corner. The water wheel spins by default and sends rotation west along a shaft; the windmill does the same to the north. Each shaft carries its rotation into a gear, and the two gears mesh perpendicular at the corner, so both sources turn the same coupled pair. A compact sampler of the rotation system — two power sources, shafts, and a gear corner in a single build.

showcases.name: Motor → Reverser → Mechanical Piston
showcases.blurb: A motor drives a mechanical piston through a reverser; two poles give it a two-block reach that shoves an oak log.
showcases.description: The mechanical piston is a rotation-powered ram. A passive motor feeds power through a reverser and a shaft into the piston core; the core doesn't care which side the power comes from — it draws from whichever shaft sits against it. Clockwise spin slides the rod out and counter-clockwise pulls it back, and the reach is set by how many poles stack behind the core: two here, so it throws two blocks (a "double" reach). The sticky head carries the oak log in front of it along for the ride. A floor lever powers the reverser to flip the spin direction and switch the stroke between extend and retract; it is shown here in the off position, so the rod is driving out.

showcases.name: Windmill → Chain Pulleys → Fan
showcases.blurb: Three chain-linked pulleys form a closed loop that carries a windmill's power across two gaps to spin a fan.
showcases.description: A chain pulley jumps rotational power across a gap with no shaft between the two ends — link one to another with a chain and, once the links close into a loop, power flows all the way around; an open chain renders but carries nothing. Here a windmill feeds the first pulley directly below it, that pulley's chain reaches a second, the second's chain reaches a third, and the third's chain closes the loop back to the first. A gear and fan sit above the third pulley, drawing off the loop's power just like they would from an ordinary shaft. Each live chain link also costs a little power of its own (more for a longer span), so a loop this size needs a real source, not just a redstone motor.

showcases.name: Steam Sieve
showcases.blurb: Water wheels drive pumps that feed a boiler and a sieve; the steam stack above works the sieve through an overhead gear bridge.
showcases.description: The full water-and-steam production chain. Three water wheels ride a stone-walled stream and gear their rotation west through a redstone dynamo into a pair of pumps: one pump lifts water through copper pipes into the boiler, the other feeds the sieve's supply line. A burner under the boiler turns that water into steam, and the steam piston on top drives the roof shaft run — north along the top and down an overhead gear bridge into the sieve, which shakes its contents down into barrels. A clutch branch south of the stack, gated by a redstone torch, ties the roof run into the pump train, and the dynamo's output feeds a comparator circuit with a digital power readout. An engine on the wheel axle stands by as backup power, plumbed to a fuel barrel.

showcases.name: Crane
showcases.blurb: A working tower crane: a redstone motor drives a shaft column up through a gearbox and a ceiling rotator to a chain hoist that raises and lowers its load.
showcases.description: A vertical crane assembled entirely from the mechanism set. At the base, stacked redstone motors feed a reverser and a long vertical shaft column running up through the stone-brick-and- spruce tower. Near the top the power turns a corner through a bank of gears and an acacia gearbox, then a ceiling-mounted rotator hands it off to the horizontal boom. Out along the copper-clad arm, gearboxes carry the drive to a chain hoist whose iron chain raises and lowers the load. Levers, repeaters and redstone torches on the control wall gate the motors so the arm can be started, stopped and reversed.
